new_statements.quote: My premise here is that the Middle Greek accentuation of foreign names can be treated seriously. Based on this hypothesis, one arrives at the following conclusions : (a) Two-syllable words that were not clear etymologically to the speakers had the stress on the ultima: adám, donát, qará, mungúq (but, interestingly enough, munğu ~ munğü). (b) Two-syllable words that were transparent, rightly or not, to the speaker had the stress on the penúltima (stem) : ögä ( < ö-), öldin ( < öl-), bérik, oktär, gésam (or gesmi), múngu (< Chinese loanword). (c) Suffixes were divided into two groups: (1) stressed and (2) non-stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Section C.IV.3 'Stress' (p. 469) states stress placement for the reconstructed Hunnic words on the premise that Middle Greek accent marks on the transcribed names are reliable: etymologically opaque disyllables are stressed on the ultima (adám, donát, qará, mungúq), transparent disyllables on the penult = stem (ögä, öldin, bérik, oktär, gésam, múngu), suffixes fall into stressed (/ÁK/, /ćiG/, /siG/, /ćUr/, /Á/, /GÄsi/) and unstressed (/lA/, /Gir/, /GAn/, /DA/, /Din/, /GUn/) classes, and compounds are stressed on each member or on the second member (penult if disyllabic: es qám, ata qám, attíla), sole exception qará tön. Earlier (p. 466, vocalism) the neutral vowel in closed syllables 'has a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed Danubian Hunnic (Attila clan, 5th c.), inferred from Greek accent marks: stress is lexically/morphologically conditioned -- final in opaque disyllables, on the stem (penult) in transparent ones, with a class of inherently stressed suffixes attracting stress and a class of unstressed suffixes leaving it on the stem; compounds stress the second member (its penult if disyllabic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; compounds may carry a stress 'on each component' (öy bárs).
new_statements.exceptions: qará tön keeps stress on the ultima of the first member ('not yet considered to be a true composite noun'); munğu ~ munğü accent variation; múngu penult-stressed as a Chinese loanword.
new_statements.identity_note: PASS-1 WORK, added: open Internet Archive copy downloaded (whole-issue PDF, text) and read; pass 1 and A never opened it. Its object is the language of Attila's dynasty and officers (ca. 370-470 AD, Danube), reconstructed from 33 names in Priscus, Jordanes etc. and classed by Pritsak as Hunno-Bulgarian (between Turkic and Mongolian). The Hsiung-nu/Xiongnu of the Chinese records (= xion1234, Mongolia, 3rd c. BC-2nd c. AD) are never mentioned in the article; whether European Hunnic continues the Xiongnu language is an open hypothesis (pro: Bonmann & Fries 2025, as Yeniseian; contra Pritsak's own Altaic reading), and Glottolog has no separate Hunnic languoid. Hence 'unclear': this is a stress statement about Danubian Hunnic, NOT about Xiong-Nu, and must not be filed under xion1234 without an identity ruling.
